description: Across eight quantitative studies (N = 3,413), a meta-analysis found a small-to-moderate positive association between traditional machismo and depressive symptoms (r = .243), with a similar correlation for broader emotional distress (r = .250).

aspect: EXAMPLE - and it does not increase willingness to get help
description: A scoping review reports higher machismo endorsement linked to depression, stress, PTSD and suicidal ideation, and to lower rates of seeking mental health care - with evidence that machismo was linked to higher depressive symptoms but NOT to greater willingness to seek services, in both Mexican men and women.
energy_note: More symptoms, and no more likely to ask.

aspect: EXAMPLE - the literature distinguishes two things
description: Arciniega et al.'s (2008) Traditional Machismo and Caballerismo Scale separates traditional machismo from caballerismo - a prosocial, chivalrous dimension emphasising family and honour. Treating them as one construct is a known error.
energy_note: Two constructs, routinely collapsed into one slur.

aspect: EXAMPLE - and the deficit story is too simple
description: A study of rural Mexican adults found largely positive help-seeking attitudes, often relying on familial support, with familismo connecting people to family and to services. Getrich et al. found machismo did not negatively affect colonoscopy screening. One study of Mexican American veterans found machismo related to both positive and negative mental health outcomes.
energy_note: It also holds families together, which is why it persists.

description: Because machismo intersects with other social systems and spans multiple sub-domains, isolating its independent role in Latino mental health has proven difficult. The association is real and the causal share is not established.
energy_note: Real, and not cleanly separable from poverty.
